::: {.why}
Every backtest you write for the next eleven months assumes an order type, usually without saying so, and today is where you learn what you would be assuming.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- State exactly what a limit order, a market order, a stop order and a stop-limit order instruct the exchange to do, in the exchange's terms rather than the broker's marketing.
- Say which of those four can execute at a price you did not choose, and which can fail to execute at all.

::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [40 min]{.task-min} Watch lectures 1 and 2 of the Copenhagen Financial Markets Microstructure playlist, following along in the matching slides from the finmarkets repository. This is the cleanest free treatment of the book and the order types.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [15 min]{.task-min} Write the four order types into the glossary as instructions, in the form: if the book looks like this, do that. Then add the two failure modes: the limit order that never fills, and the stop that fills 3 percent below where you set it.

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
Four order-type entries in the glossary, each written as an instruction to a matching engine, each with its failure mode.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
You place a market order to buy 10,000 shares of a stock quoted 20.00 bid, 20.02 offered with 300 shares showing. What price do you get?
:::
